hypothesis: For every one-dimensional local constraint system (a set of allowed length-w colour words over k colours) that admits any bi-infinite satisfying arrangement, there is a purely periodic satisfying arrangement, and its period can be taken at most V = k^(w-1).
pass_criterion: Pre-registered: across all enumerated or sampled constraint systems, every system that admits a valid word of length 4V + w (the operational test of satisfiability, independent of any cycle argument) also admits a periodic arrangement u^infinity with |u| <= V whose every cyclic window of length w is allowed; and every system with no such long valid word has no periodic arrangement either. Zero violations in both directions.
fail_criterion: Pre-registered: at least one constraint system admits a valid word of length 4V + w but no periodic arrangement with period <= V (this would refute the claim as stated, since the shortest possible periodic solution is bounded by V); or the two satisfiability indicators disagree in the other direction, which would indicate a broken test.
interpretation: Wolfram's 'local set of constraints' on a one-dimensional array of coloured cells (p. 210-211: each cell's neighbourhood must be one of a given set of allowed configurations) is a one-dimensional subshift of finite type: a set of allowed words of a fixed window length w over k colours. 'Can be satisfied at all' is read as the existence of a bi-infinite arrangement all of whose windows are allowed; by compactness this is equivalent to the existence of arbitrarily long valid finite words, and operationally it is tested by the existence of a valid word of length 4V + w (any valid word longer than V must revisit a de Bruijn vertex, so this length is far beyond the threshold, and the check is done by a reachability iteration, not a cycle search). 'Simple and purely repetitive arrangement' is read as a periodic configuration, found by brute-force enumeration of all period words u with |u| <= V = k^(w-1) and checking all cyclic windows. All constraint systems are enumerated exhaustively for (k, w) in {(2,2), (2,3), (2,4), (3,2), (4,2)} and sampled with a fixed seed for (2,5) and (3,3).
